title: Scheduling your training for Blue Collar workers
summary: How manual laborers should schedule training around their job. Work comes before training, so blue-collar workers should do short, intense compound sessions leaving reps in the tank, skip body parts their job already trains, put most volume on days off and use flexible substitutions around heavy work days.
claims: His priorities are family first, work second, training third
Blue-collar training must never impair the ability to do hard work every day
Construction is like low-intensity, high-volume, high-frequency training and drains the cardiovascular system
Construction workers should train with short sessions of intense low-rep sets on a few key compounds
White-collar workers can work injured; manual laborers can't, so avoiding injury is key
Use reps in the tank: around 4-6 or 2-4 reps; on deadlifts stop at 2 when 3-4 were possible
Body parts your job trains heavily, like a welder's forearms and shoulders, may need no direct training
Some of the biggest forearms he has seen belong to welders, not gym bros
Welders should reinforce their lower back because posture at work degrades the spine
Roofers may need less leg training, but strength work still helps by covering movement patterns the job misses
Even with a grip-heavy job, use straps or brief heavy holds like one heavy rack pull held until it slips
Work-training cycles must be skewed toward work; if overuse injuries build, replace training with rehab
Blue-collar workers should put most volume on days off and keep weekdays to minimal strength work, the opposite of white-collar workers
Plan around known strenuous work days so you're 100% fresh for them
A good minimalist program is minimalist from necessity, not laziness, and stays flexible
Keep a pre-planned easier swap, like back extensions or light RDLs, for heavy deadlifts when the next work day needs your back
His grandfather worked construction 7 days a week for about 35 years without lifting thanks to a short, tanky build
Tall people are more prone to lower back and knee issues
Blue-collar workers still need strength training because their job only trains certain qualities
Blue-collar workers don't need much cardio; white-collar desk workers need more
exercises: one heavy set held until grip slips
